hints: Write the hypotheses in terms of the population mean $\mu$ (the weekly income). $\text{H}_0$ keeps the old mean, 546. $\text{H}_1$ says the income has increased: which way does that point, and is it one-tailed or two-tailed?
The sample has 40 weeks and $\sigma = 120$ is known, so the sample mean is normal with standard deviation $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$. Standardise: $z = \dfrac{581 - 546}{120/\sqrt{40}}$.
On a calculator put brackets round the whole denominator: (581 - 546) / (120 / $\sqrt{40}$). Work out $z$ and keep at least 3 significant figures.
This is a one-tailed test at 2.5%, so the critical value is the $z$ with 2.5% in the upper tail, that is $\Phi(z) = 0.975$. Compare your $z$ with it.
Decide whether your $z$ lies in the rejection region or not, and then write the conclusion in the context of Bob's weekly income, using 'there is (no) evidence that...', not a definite statement.
walkthrough:
**Hypotheses (B1)**

$\mu$ means the (population) mean weekly income of Bob now. Before the change it was \$546, so $\text{H}_0$ says nothing has changed. Bob thinks it has **increased**, so $\text{H}_1$ is one-tailed with '$>$':

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 546$$

$$\text{H}_1: \mu > 546$$

You need both for the B1.

**Distribution of the sample mean under H0**

If $\text{H}_0$ is true, individual incomes have mean 546 and standard deviation 120. We have the mean $\bar{x}$ of a sample of $n = 40$ weeks. For a large sample, the central limit theorem says $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal:

$$\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(546, \frac{120^2}{40}\right)$$

The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$, not 120, because averages of 40 weeks vary much less than single weeks:

$$\sqrt{40} = 6.32456 \qquad \frac{120}{6.32456} = 18.9737$$

**Test statistic (M1 and A1)**

Standardise the observed sample mean 581:

$$z = \frac{581 - 546}{\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}}$$

This earns the M1 (it must contain $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$). Now the numbers:

$$581 - 546 = 35$$

$$z = \frac{35}{18.9737} = 1.8447$$

So $z = 1.845$ (the scheme also allows 1.844, 1.84 or 1.85). This earns the A1.

**Compare with the critical value (second M1)**

The test is one-tailed at 2.5%, so the rejection region is the top 2.5% of the normal curve. The $z$ value with 0.975 below it is

$$\Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96$$

We compare our value:

$$1.845 < 1.96$$

Our $z$ is not in the rejection region. (Equivalent: $\text{P}(Z > 1.845) = 0.0325$, which is bigger than 0.025.) This earns the M1.

**Conclusion in context (A1FT)**

Because $1.845 < 1.96$ we do not reject $\text{H}_0$. In words, with no definite claim:

There is **no evidence**, at the 2.5% level, that Bob's mean weekly income has increased.

Note that this does not prove it has stayed the same. Common slip: using a two-tailed critical value, which is not right here as the question asks about an increase.

**Final answer**

$z = 1.845 < 1.96$, so we do not reject $\text{H}_0$: there is no evidence that Bob's mean weekly income has increased.

hints: A Type II error means accepting $\text{H}_0$ when it is actually false (the true mean is 595). First find the boundary of the acceptance region in terms of the sample mean: call it $a$, the value of $\bar{x}$ that gives exactly the critical $z$, using the mean 546 from $\text{H}_0$.
Set $\dfrac{a - 546}{120/\sqrt{40}} = 1.96$ (the 2.5% one-tailed critical value) and rearrange: $a = 546 + 1.96 \times \dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$. Work it out.

$\text{H}_0$ is accepted when $\bar{x} < a$. Now the sample mean really comes from a population with mean 595 (same $\sigma$, same 40 weeks), so standardise your boundary using 595: $z = \dfrac{a - 595}{120/\sqrt{40}}$.
You want $\text{P}(\bar{X} < a)$, the area to the left of that $z$. If your $z$ is negative, the area to the left is a small tail, equal to $1 - \Phi(|z|)$.
Find $\Phi(|z|)$ from the normal table or your calculator, subtract from 1 (or use normal cdf directly) and round to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
**What a Type II error is here**

A **Type II error** happens when we accept $\text{H}_0$ although it is false. Here $\text{H}_0$ is $\mu = 546$, but the true mean is now 595. So we need the probability that the sample mean lands in the 'accept $\text{H}_0$' region even though the true mean is 595.

The test is the same as in (i): one-tailed, 2.5% level, $n = 40$, $\sigma = 120$.

**Find the boundary of the acceptance region (M1 and A1)**

We reject $\text{H}_0$ when $z > 1.96$. The boundary is the sample mean $a$ with exactly $z = 1.96$, **calculated using the $\text{H}_0$ mean 546**:

$$\frac{a - 546}{\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}} = 1.96$$

This earns the M1 (it needs $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$, 546 and a $z$ value). Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}} = 18.9737$:

$$a - 546 = 1.96 \times 18.9737 = 37.1884$$

$$a = 546 + 37.1884 = 583.1884 \approx 583.19$$

This earns the A1 (583 to 3 s.f. is allowed). So we accept $\text{H}_0$ when $\bar{x} < 583.19$.

**Standardise using the true mean 595 (third M1)**

Now the sample mean $\bar{X}$ has the true distribution: mean 595, standard deviation $\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}$. A Type II error is $\text{P}(\bar{X} < 583.19)$. Standardise with 595:

$$z = \frac{583.19 - 595}{\dfrac{120}{\sqrt{40}}}$$

$$583.19 - 595 = -11.81$$

$$z = \frac{-11.81}{18.9737} = -0.6224 \approx -0.622$$

This earns the M1. Slip to avoid: using 546 here instead of 595.

**Find the probability (last M1 and A1)**

We want the area to the left of $z = -0.622$: a small tail on the left of the bell curve (sketch it). By symmetry it equals the area to the right of $+0.622$:

$$\text{P}(Z < -0.622) = 1 - \Phi(0.622)$$

This earns the M1 (a consistent area). Use the normal table or your calculator's normal cdf:

$$\Phi(0.622) = 0.7330$$

$$1 - 0.7330 = 0.2670$$

To 3 significant figures this is 0.267. This earns the A1.

**Final answer**

The probability of a Type II error is **0.267** (3 s.f.).
